newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 28.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Following continuation of a political deadlock in a weekend meeting of key National Party and farm leaders aimed at discussing how Federal legislation could allow the States to deal with problems arising from the High Court's controversial Wik decision, Pime Minister John Howard vowed yesterday to press ahead with his 10-point Native Title plan. Page 1.

In a move aimed primarily at helping rural Victoria, the State Government has announced it will cut diesel and petrol taxes by A$106 million in tomorrow's Victorian Budget, with the reductions to come into effect on June 1. State Premier Jeff Kennett said the Budget would see Victoria's franchise fees fall to 7.5 cents a litre for diesel and 7.8 cents for petrol. Page 3.

Speaking on Network Ten's Meet the Press program on the eve of a two-day visit by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto yesterday, Federal Defence Minister Ian McLachlan revealed Australia plans to step up its defence links with Japan, but stressed that any increase in ties would be done in a way that both Australia and Japan "feel comfortable with". Page 5.

Following a weekend media report which alleged that four left-wing union officials were involved in a "serious push" to have ACTU secretary Bill Kelty removed, senior left-wing officials strongly denied yesterday that there were any moves under way within the Left to oust Kelty from his current position. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Under Prime Minister John Howard's 10-point response to the High Court's controversial Wik ruling, States would be able to remove Aborigines' special powers over development projects and in some cases force them to relinquish native title rights over pastoral leases through compulsory land acquisition, but the States would also be responsible for compensation involved in the compulsory land acquisitions. Page 1.

On the eve of the one-year anniversary of the Port Arthur massacre, the chief executive officer of the Port Arthur Historic Site management authority, Craig Coombs, inflamed emotions yesterday when he told The Australian that the wooden cross memorial marking the deaths of the 35 victims is to be removed, perhaps to the bush behind the Broad Arrow Cafe. Page 1.

Federal Trade Minister Tim Fischer told the Nine Network's Sunday program yesterday he is confident Australia can gain greater access to Japan's lucrative rice market during talks with Japanese Prime Minister Hashimoto, who is visiting Australia today to ark the 40th anniversary of the 1957 Australia-Japan trade treaty. Page 1.

According to an analysis of a housing report by the economic forecaster BIS Shrapnel, median house prices in Melbourne and Sydney will increase 40 per cent over the next three years thanks to a combination of low interest rates, stock shortages and perception the housing markets in the two cities were undervalued. However it is predicted that prices will then decrease sharply because of over-supply. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

According to the Federal Opposition and privacy experts, including Australian Privacy Foundation director Tim Dixon, the Howard Government's decision to transfer computer processing of personal records - including tax, health, law enforcement and welfare nformation - to the private sector could threaten the privacy of millions of Australians. Page 1.

Speaking on Channel Ten's Meet the Press program yesterday, Federal Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said the Korean peninsula was in a "parlous state", with reports that people were now starving, and he signalled Australia will consider sending forces to hlp South Korea if unstable North Korea launches a desperate attack. Page 1.

According to a survey by Outbound Newspapers, which publishes information for immigrants, one in three people now thinking of leaving Britain would definitely make the move if the Conservatives get re-elected, and many of those would go to Australia, with the Australian High Commission in London revealing there has been a significant increase recently in inquiries about emigrating. Page 1.

Australian Olympic Committee president, John Coates, claims the anti-immigration campaign being run by Independent MP Pauline Hanson on behalf of her new One Nation party, is "regularly raised" with Australian Olympic officials during their overseas visit. "We've just got to make sure....it's explained that this (stance) doesn't represent mainstream Australia" he said. Page 3.
THE AGE

Political, church and civic figures will lead remembrance services around Australia today on the first anniversary of the Port Arthur massacre, in which 35 people lost their lives. Governor-General, Sir William Deane, is to attend a commemorative service organised by locals at the Port Arthur site. Page A1.

According to a study of 420 women at six, 12, 18 and 24 weeks after birth by Sydney University's department of psychological medicine at Nepean Hospital, women leaving hospital less than three days after giving birth are at greater risk of developing severe depression. Page A1.

Victorians will pay less for petrol and diesel from June 1 under a A$106 million tax cut unveiled by Premier Jeff Kennett yesterday and welcomed by the RACV and the Victorian Farmers Federation. Kennett said the Government would take action against wholeslers and retailers if the cuts of up to 4.1 cents a litre on diesel and 1.6 cents a litre on petrol, were not passed on in full from June 1. Page A1.

Following calls for a royal commission into MAS contract deals, it has been revealed top ambulance service officials were warned of serious "functional and technical shortcomings" in the specifications for a computer dispatch system, in a report prepared by Henderson Consultants, a month before Intergraph won the lucrative contract. Page A3.
